abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating condition with limited therapeutic options and a strong neuroinflammatory component that exacerbates tissue damage and impairs functional recovery. Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a histone methyltransferase and core component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), has emerged as a key regulator of epigenetic modifications involved in neuroinflammation. In this study, we investigated the potential neuroprotective effects of GSK‐343, a selective EZH2 inhibitor, in a murine model of SCI induced by extradural compression. Female adult CD1 mice received intraperitoneal injections of GSK‐343 (1, 5, or 10 mg/kg) at 1‐ and 6‐h post‐injury. After 24 h, spinal cord tissues were collected and analyzed. GSK‐343 treatment significantly reduced histological damage, neuronal demyelination, and the expression of pro‐inflammatory markers, likely through modulation of the TRAF6/NF‐κB signaling pathway. Moreover, EZH2 inhibition attenuated innate immune responses, as evidenced by the reduction in mast cell infiltration, microglial activation, and MCP‐1 levels. These findings support the therapeutic potential of EZH2 inhibition as a novel epigenetic strategy to counteract neuroinflammation and promote early neuroprotection following SCI.

sec.p: Keywords: enhancer of zeste homolog 2, GSK‐343, innate immunity, neuroinflammation, spinal cord injury

list-item.p: Spinal cord injury (SCI) triggers a rapid and sustained neuroinflammatory response that contributes to secondary damage and impairs neurological recovery.
Epigenetic regulation, particularly via the histone methyltransferase EZH2, has emerged as a key modulator of these pathological events.

In this study, we provide the first evidence that pharmacological inhibition of EZH2 with GSK‐343 attenuates early neuroinflammation, demyelination, and innate immune cell activation following acute SCI in mice.

Our findings highlight EZH2 as a promising epigenetic target to modulate the TRAF6/NF‐κB pathway and control inflammation‐driven damage, offering a potential new therapeutic avenue for SCI management.

abstract.p: In a mouse model of spinal cord injury, pharmacological inhibition of EZH2 with GSK‐343 reduces tissue damage and neuronal demyelination. GSK‐343 suppresses the EZH2/TRAF6/NF‐κB signaling pathway, leading to attenuation of neuroinflammation and innate immune activation. These effects promote early neuroprotection and improved locomotor recovery in vivo.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is one of the most debilitating injuries that can result in permanent paralysis and, in extreme circumstances, death. SCI is caused by severe damage to the axons that pass through the spinal cord, with typical effects such as loss of motor and sensory function significantly worsening patients' quality of life (Eckert and Martin 2017). With an incidence ranging from 3.6 to 195.4 patients per million worldwide, SCI is generally caused by fairly traumatic events such as automobile collisions, falls, or sports injuries (National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center 2016). Unfortunately, to date, there is no adequate medical treatment capable of restoring the serious damage (Karsy and Hawryluk 2019). The most suitable pharmacological treatment is methylprednisolone sodium succinate, a drug that increases antioxidant defenses but is not able to improve functional recovery, axon remyelination, and neurite sprouting (Ito et al. 2009). Therefore, one of the main goals of research is to develop new pharmacological approaches for patients with SCI. Trauma consists of primary and secondary phases: firstly, irreversible mechanical damage to spinal cord tissue that occurs immediately after impact is known as “primary” injury, while “secondary” injury occurs for a few days or months and ultimately causes more serious consequences (Alizadeh et al. 2019). From the point of view of etiopathogenesis, it has been demonstrated that immediately after spinal cord trauma there is a sudden increase in the infiltration of leukocytes and activation of glial cells, which exacerbate tissue damage by releasing proteases, lysosomal enzymes, and proinflammatory substances into the damaged site (Alizadeh et al. 2019). This abnormal inflammatory reaction promotes neuronal death, inhibits the growth of scar tissue, and modifies the physiological balance of several endogenous variables, worsening traumatic damage (Oyinbo 2011). Neuroinflammatory damage, firstly, promotes the activation of the nuclear transcription factor, nuclear factor‐kappa B (NF‐κB) which drives the release of numerous proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin 1‐β (IL‐1β), IL‐17, tumor necrosis factor α (TNF‐α) and other cytotoxic factors (Rust and Kaiser 2017). Furthermore, within 24 h of trauma, released pro‐inflammatory markers promote the activation of resident innate immune cells that contribute to spinal cord damage (Schnell et al. 1999). Among these, microglial cells, the main immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS), once activated, stimulate the production of substances that increase the sensation of pain (Sun et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2018). Indeed, innate immunity and inflammation are closely associated with the pathogenesis of SCI, influencing each other's physiological responses (Papatheodorou et al. 2017). Therefore, a new therapeutic approach could aim to mitigate inflammation and innate immunity system activation to promote more effective healing.

Recent research on epigenetic mechanisms demonstrated that several neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory disorders exhibit dysregulated DNA methylation and post‐translational modifications of histones, essential for gene expression in nearly all tissues, and are strongly linked to neuroinflammation processes (Neal and Richardson 2018; Chatterjee et al. 2017). In the onset and maintenance of spinal cord trauma, epigenetic processes such as DNA methylation, histone modification, and non‐coding RNAs are involved in the activation and repression of different gene expressions (Zhang et al. 2020). In this context, much attention has been paid to the enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) which is an essential component of polycomb complex 2 (PRC2), a repressive epigenetic transcriptional regulator of genes. EZH2 acts as a methyltransferase and causes gene silencing by adding mono‐, di‐, or tri‐methyl groups to histone 27 (H3K27) (Alam et al. 2015). Its methyltransferase action leads to gene silencing (Cao et al. 2008), causing the inactivation of the expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 (Socs3), which determines the uncontrollable activation of NF‐κB, promoting the production of pro‐inflammatory genes (Zhang et al. 2018). EZH2 not only plays its role in regulating inflammation, but recent studies showed that it could also influence the functions of the immune system (Tumes et al. 2013; Stairiker et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2018; Mannino et al. 2023). Indeed, hematopoietic stem cell activity and lymphocyte development might depend on EZH2 and other PRC2 components because they suppress cell cycle inhibitors. Furthermore, it was observed that silencing of EZH2 suppressed the pro‐inflammatory response in macrophages/microglia in a mouse model of colitis (Zhang et al. 2018). Moreover, in the field of the CNS, EZH2 is predominantly expressed in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and plays a fundamental role in the development and maintenance of neuropathic pain through the regulation of the neuroinflammation process (Yadav and Weng 2017).

In the last years several strong and extremely selective EZH2 methyltransferase activity inhibitors, such as GSK126 and GSK‐343, have been developed. Particularly, GSK‐343 (1‐isopropyl‐1H‐indazole‐4‐carboxamide) is a member of the class of indazoles and it is a competitive inhibitor of methionine histone lysine methyltransferase EZH2, tested for several cancer such as ovarian cancer, osteosarcoma, neuroblastoma and glioma (Amatangelo et al. 2013; Xiong et al. 2020; Yu et al. 2017; Wang, Xu, et al. 2020; Scuderi et al. 2022). Pharmacokinetic studies conducted on this molecule showed that the class of compounds to which GSK343 belongs easily crosses the blood–brain barrier (BBB) (Ratnam et al. 2021). Therefore, considering the involvement of EZH2 in neuroinflammation processes and the activation of innate immunity, we aimed to evaluate the neuroprotective abilities of GSK‐343, in an acute murine model of SCI induced by extradural compression of the spinal cord, to report, for the first time, the inhibitory effect of EZH2 on tissue regeneration and the management of the neuroinflammatory signaling pathways underlying this pathology.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: GSK‐343 was purchased by Sigma‐Aldrich (Bristol, UK). Unless otherwise indicated, all compounds were obtained from Sigma‐Aldrich Company Ltd. (Milan, Italy). All stock solutions were prepared in non‐pyrogenic saline (0.9% NaCl; Baxter, Italy, UK). GSK‐343 was dissolved in a saline solution.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Female adult CD1 mice, 8 weeks old (25–30 g, Envigo, Udine, Italy), were housed in a controlled environment and provided with standard rodent chow and water, in stainless steel cages in a room kept at 22°C ± 1°C with a 12‐h light and 12‐h dark cycle. Adult female CD1 mice were used to minimize the behavioral and inflammatory variability typical of males and to ensure greater stability in the response to spinal injury during the acute phase. Only healthy adult female CD1 mice weighing 25 to 30 g were included in the study. Animals with signs of disease, pre‐existing spinal malformations, or that showed no obvious signs of damage after induction of spinal cord injury were excluded. This study was performed following Italian regulations on the use of animals (D.M.116192) and Directive legislation (EU) (2010/63/EU) amended by Regulation (EU) 2019/1010 and ARRIVE guidelines. Moreover, the study was approved by the OPBA of Messina with the authorization number 399/2019‐PR.

sec.title: Surgical Procedure for SCI
sec.p: After anesthesia, to perform SCI, a longitudinal incision in the midline of the back of mice was made to expose the paravertebral muscles and spine at the T5 and T8 tracts (Filippone et al. 2020). Next, the upper and lower vertebrae were pierced, exposing the spinal cord. After laminectomy, the spinal cord lesion was produced by extradural compression of the spinal cord from T6 to T7 using an aneurysm clip with a closing force of 24 g for 1 min. During recovery from anesthesia, the mice were placed on a warm heating pad and covered with a warm towel. Twenty‐four hours after the SCI procedure, spinal cord tissues were collected and used for further analyses. Sham mice were only subjected to laminectomy. GSK‐343 intraperitoneal (ip) treatments at the doses of 1, 5, and 10 mg/kg were administered 1 and 6 h post the SCI procedure. The doses of GSK343 were chosen based on the previous studies (Mannino et al. 2023). The animal study protocol was approved by OPBA the University of Messina review board for the care of animals with the authorization number 399/2019‐PR.

sec.title: Experimental Groups
sec.p: Mice were randomly divided as follows:

list-item.p: Sham + Vehicle: mice were subjected to laminectomy, but the aneurysm clip was not applied; these mice were administered with saline solution 24 h after laminectomy (n = 10).
SCI + Vehicle: mice were subjected to SCI plus ip administration of saline solution (n = 10).
SCI + GSK‐343 (1 mg/kg): mice were subjected to SCI followed by ip administration of GSK‐343 1 mg/kg 1 and 6 h after SCI (n = 10).
SCI + GSK‐343 (5 mg/kg): mice were subjected to SCI followed by ip administration of GSK‐343 5 mg/kg 1 and 6 h after SCI (n = 10).
SCI + GSK‐343 (10 mg/kg): mice were subjected to SCI followed by ip administration of GSK‐343 10 mg/kg 1 and 6 h after SCI (n = 10).

sec.title: Histological Evaluation
sec.p: Twenty‐four hours after SCI, spinal cord tissues were collected and fixed in 10% (w/v) PBS‐buffered formaldehyde solution at 25°C for 24 h, dehydrated with graduated ethanol, and embedded in paraffin (obtaining 7‐μm thick sections). Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed to investigate histological damage and loss of tissue architecture in the perilesional area of spinal cord tissues. The histological score followed a five‐point scale based on the following morphological criteria: (0) no pathological abnormalities; (1) small, scattered areas of axonal swelling, morphologically unremarkable tissue in > 75% of the perilesional area; (2) significant damage with normal gross architecture, unremarkable tissue in 50%–75% of the perilesional area; (3) significant damage with normal gross architecture, morphologically unremarkable tissue in 25%–50% of perilesional area; (4) significant damage and loss of gross architecture in large areas, morphologically unremarkable tissue in 10% –25% of perilesional area; (5) complete dissolution of the spinal cord tissue over the entire perilesional area with loss of gross architecture, morphologically unremarkable tissue in < 10% of perilesional area. “ND” (not detectable) indicates values below the limit of detection of the assay, rather than an absolute zero. For statistical purposes, all analyses were performed on the raw numerical data. For each animal, three sagittal sections of the spinal cord were analyzed, and the obtained mean was used for statistical evaluation. In addition to the histological injury score (0–5), edema and neutrophil infiltration were also evaluated on H&E‐stained spinal cord sections. Edema was scored using a five‐grade scale (0–4) based on the extent of vacuolization and interstitial space expansion in the perilesional area (0 = no edema, 1 = slight, 2 = moderate, 3 = severe, 4 = extensive edema with diffuse tissue disruption) (Bravo‐Reyna et al. 2025). Instead, neutrophil infiltration was quantified by counting the number of neutrophil cells/field using ImageJ software (version 1.53a). Sections were examined by light microscopy (Nikon Eclipse Ci‐L microscope, NIKON CORPORATION, Tokyo, Japan) employing an objective lens of 20× and 40×. Histological scoring was performed following a five‐point scale based on specific morphological criteria (Paterniti et al. 2023).

sec.title: Luxol Fast Blue (LFB) Staining
sec.p: Luxol fast blue (LFB) staining (Abcam, Waltham, MA 02453, USA # ab150675) was performed according to the manufacturer's guidelines (Ardizzone et al. 2023). The spinal cord sections were incubated in LFB solution at 56°C overnight, then washed in 95% alcohol. The sections were then incubated in a lithium carbonate solution and 70% ethyl alcohol, and finally counterstained with cresyl violet solution. After dehydration, the sections were mounted with Eukitt (Bio‐Optica, Milan, Italy). LFB positive counts were observed and counted in the perilesional area of the spinal cord by light microscopy (Nikon Eclipse Ci‐L microscope, NIKON CORPORATION, Tokyo, Japan).

sec.title: Western Blot Analysis of EZH2, TRAF6, NF‐kB, IL‐1b, IL‐17, COX2, iNOS, and CD45
sec.p: For western blot analysis, the samples were processed with Lysis Buffers for the extraction of nucleated and cytosolic proteins, as described previously (Cucinotta et al. 2023). Particularly, cytosolic extracts were obtained by treating the spinal cord section with Buffer A containing protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma Cat. N. P8340), sucrose 1 M, Tris HCl 1 M, EGTA 100 mM, EDTA 100 mM, NaN3 100 mM, β‐Mercaptoethanol 14.3 M, NaF 0.5 M homogenized at the highest setting for 2 min, and centrifuged at 1000× g for 10 min at 4°C. Supernatants represented the cytosolic fraction. Pellets, containing enriched nuclei, were resuspended in buffer B containing protease inhibitor cocktail, 1% Triton X‐100, NaCl 5 M, Tris HCl 10 mM, EGTA 100 mM, EDTA 100 mM, After centrifugation at 15,000× g for 30 min at 4°C, supernatants containing the nuclear protein were stored at −80°C for further analysis. After the electrophoretic run, the membranes were incubated at 4°C overnight (O/N) with primary antibodies diluted in milk, Phospahate‐Buffered Saline (PBS), and 0.1% Tween‐20 (PMT). Anti‐EZH2 (1:500; Invitrogen MA5‐15101), anti‐Histone H3 dimethyl Lys27 (H3K27Me2) (1:500; Invitrogen 39245), anti‐TRAF6 (1:500; sc‐8409, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), anti‐ IkB‐a (1:500; sc‐1643: Santa Cruz Biotechnology); anti‐NF‐kB (1:500; sc‐8008; Santa Cruz Biotechnology); anti‐COX‐2 (1:500; sc‐376861; Santa Cruz Biotechnology); anti‐iNOS (1:500; sc‐7271; Santa Cruz Biotechnology); anti‐IL‐1b (1:500; sc‐515598; Santa Cruz Biotechnology); anti‐IL‐17 (1:500; sc‐374,218; Santa Cruz Biotechnology); anti‐TNF‐α (1:500; sc‐52746, Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA, USA); anti‐CD45 (1:500; sc‐19597; Santa Cruz Biotechnology). The stripping and re‐probing of the western blot membrane were performed to detect some antibodies. To confirm that the samples contained an equal protein concentration, membranes were incubated with primary anti‐β‐actin antibody (1:500; sc‐47778; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA) for the cytosolic fraction or LAMIN A (1:500; sc‐518013; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Dallas, TX, USA) for the nuclear fraction. Finally, membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with a secondary anti‐mouse antibody (1:1000, Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories; West Grove, PA, USA; cat#115‐035‐068) or a secondary anti‐rabbit antibody (1:1000, Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories; West Grove, PA, USA, cat#111‐035‐003). The bands were obtained using a chemiluminescence detection system (ECL) according to the manufacturer's instructions (Thermo, Waltham, MA, USA). The relative expression of the protein bands was quantified by densitometry with the Bio‐Rad ChemiDocTMXRS+ software and standardized to β‐actin or LAMIN A levels as internal controls. Western blot images were analyzed using ImageJ software (version 1.53a). For each band, a region of interest was manually selected. The integrated density values were collected for each band and normalized to the corresponding housekeeping protein (β‐actin for cytosolic extracts or Lamin A for nuclear extracts).

sec.title: Immunofluorescence Staining of GFAP and IBA‐1
sec.p: Sagittal spinal cord sections were incubated with anti‐ GFAP (1:100, sc‐9065, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) and anti‐IBA‐1 (1:100, sc‐32725, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) antibodies in a humidified chamber O/N at 37°C. Twenty‐four hours later, sections were incubated with conjugated anti‐rabbit Alexa Fluor‐488 secondary antibody #A‐32731 (1:1000 in PBS, v/v Molecular Probes, Monza, Italy) and anti‐mouse Alexa Fluor‐488 secondary antibody #A‐11001 (1:1000 in PBS, v/v Molecular Probes, Monza, Italy) for 1 h at RT. Nuclei were stained by adding 2 μg/mL 4′,6′‐diamidino‐2‐phenylindole (DAPI; Frankfurt, Germany) in PBS. For each animal, three spinal cord sections were analyzed, and the obtained mean was used for statistical evaluation. Five randomly selected fields per section at 40× magnification were evaluated in a blinded manner. Images were acquired by employing a fluorescence microscope (Nikon Eclipse Ci‐L microscope, NIKON CORPORATION, Tokyo, Japan), and the number of GFAP or IBA‐1positive cells in the perilesional area was investigated (Filippone et al. 2022).

sec.title: Blue Toluidine Staining
sec.p: The spinal cord sections were stained with toluidine blue to detect the presence of mast cells in the perilesional area, according to a previously described method (Ardizzone et al. 2022). The sections were subjected to deparaffinization using a decreasing alcohol scale, starting from xylene up to distilled water. Subsequently, the sections were stained with drops of toluidine blue, until they were completely covered, for 4 min. After which they were rinsed until clear and then dehydrated using increasing alcohols to the xylene and mounted using the Eukitt (Bio‐Optica, Milan, Italy). Mast cell count was performed on each slide using a Nikon Eclipse Ci‐L microscope. For toluidine blue staining, 40× magnification (20 μm scale bar) was shown.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry of CD68
sec.p: The expression of CD68 used as a macrophage marker around the perlesional area, was studied by immunohistochemistry analysis. Sagittal spinal cord sections were deparaffinized and rehydrated as previously described (Lanza et al. 2019). Then, the sections were incubated overnight (O/N) with primary anti‐CD68 antibody (1:100; sc‐20060; Santa Cruz Biotechnology). After, sections were washed with PBS and incubated with peroxidase‐conjugated bovine anti‐mouse immunoglobulin G (IgG). Specific labeling was detected using a biotin‐conjugated goat anti‐rabbit IgG or biotin‐conjugated goat anti‐mouse IgG and avidin‐biotin peroxidase complex (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, CA, USA). The reaction was revealed by a chromogenic substrate (brown DAB), and counterstaining with Nuclear Fast Red. Immunohistochemical images were obtained and observed using a Nikon Eclipse Ci‐L microscope. The number of positive cells (brown staining) which characterizes the percentage area of immunoreactivity, is expressed as a % of the total tissue area (red staining) with an objective lens at 20× and 40×, and the analysis was performed using ImageJ. Densitometry analysis was performed using GraphPad version 8.0 (La Jolla, CA, USA).

sec.title: Monocyte Chemotactic Protein‐1 (MCP‐1) ELISA Assay Kit
sec.p: The levels of MCP‐1 were evaluated on spinal cord tissue extract according to the manufacturer's instructions ELISA kit (Invitrogen; KRC1011; Cod no. 10692264), where the signal intensity for MCP‐1 is directly proportional to the concentration of the target present in the sample.

sec.title: BMS Open‐Field Score
sec.p: In another experimental set, the motor function of mice with spinal cord injuries was assessed, after 10 days. The open‐field score of the Basso Mouse Scale (BMS) was used to evaluate recovery from motor disruption (Li et al. 2020). The BMS scale measures locomotion on hind limb function, including weight support, stepping ability, coordination, and toe clearance. It has eight points, ranging from 0 (complete paralyzes) to 9 (normal hind limb function).

sec.title: Statistical Evaluation
sec.p: All the experimental results are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) of N observations, where N is the number of animals examined. GraphPad version 8.0 (La Jolla, CA, USA) was used for data analysis. A One‐Way ANOVA followed by a Bonferroni post hoc test for multiple comparisons was used; only a p‐value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Outliers will be identified by ROUT test. Student t‐test or Mann–Whitney test will be used to compare differences in continuous variables among groups. Each analysis was performed three times. BMS locomotor scores were analyzed using a two‐way ANOVA with repeated measures, followed by Bonferroni post hoc test. The minimum number of mice per group was estimated a priori using the G*Power software (version 3.1). The power analysis was based on a one‐way fixed‐effects ANOVA (five groups; α = 0.05; power = 0.80; effect size f = 0.40; equal group allocation), which yielded a required sample size of n = 10 animals per group. This procedure ensures an adequate statistical power to detect medium‐to‐large effects under the specified design parameters.

sec.title: GSK‐343 Treatments Restored SCI‐Induced Tissue Damage
sec.p: To investigate how GSK‐343 treatment could ameliorate tissue damage after trauma, we performed the H&E staining. The staining of the spinal cord of the SCI group revealed a significant alteration in the morphological structure of the perilesional area associated with an increase in neutrophil infiltration and edema (Figure 1B, B1, score F) compared to Sham mice (Figure 1A, A1, score F). The dose of GSK‐343 1 mg/kg was unable to restore the tissue architecture (Figure 1C, C1, score F). However, treatment with GSK‐343 at the dose of 5 mg/kg (Figure 1D, D1, score F) and even more at the dose of 10 mg/kg significantly reduced the H&E histological injury score, indicating preservation of spinal cord architecture and a decrease in tissue disorganization compared with SCI mice (Figure 1E, E1, score F). Furthermore, quantitative analyses confirmed a significant reduction in both edema score and neutrophil infiltration in mice treated with GSK‐343 at 5 and 10 mg/kg (Figure 1, panels G, H, respectively), supporting the histological evidence of tissue protection of EZH2 inhibition.

sec.title: GSK‐343 Treatments Reduced Neuronal Demyelination After SCI
sec.p: Myelin debris generated after SCI is known to inhibit axonal regeneration and remyelination. Furthermore, lipid‐laden myelin debris is taken up and processed by inflammatory cells, including neutrophils and macrophages, initiating SCI‐related inflammatory pathways (Kopper and Gensel 2018). Considering this, we used Luxol fast blue (LFB) staining to count the number of LFB‐positive neurons. The SCI groups of animals showed LFB+ neuron count significantly lower (Figure 2B, B1, score F), compared to the Sham group (Figure 2A, A1, score F), indicating that the SCI procedure induced the demyelination process in the perilesional area. Intraperitoneal treatment with GSK‐343 at 5 mg/kg showed restoration of neuron myelination (Figure 2D, D1, score F) but a greater increase in myelin recovery was observed at the highest dose of 10 mg/kg which showed an LFB+ neuron count almost comparable to the sham group (Figure 2E, E1, score F). On the contrary, LFB staining did not give positive results following GSK‐343 administration at doses of 1 mg/kg (Figure 2C, C1, score F) which was unable to restore the presence of myelin compared to SCI mice. Therefore, these results suggested that EZH2 inhibition could prevent myelin loss, exerting a neuroprotective effect after SCI.

GSK‐343 treatment at the dose of 1 mg/kg (C, C1, score F) was not effective in counteracting neuronal demyelination. Data are expressed as mean ± SD where N = 10 mice for each group. sec.title: Effect of GSK‐343 on EZH2/TRAF6/NF‐κB Pathway
sec.p: The cytosolic levels of EZH2 protein were detected by Western Blot analysis (Figure 3A, densitometric analysis A1). Results showed that EZH2 expression increased in SCI mice compared to baseline levels of sham mice. Our study demonstrated that the selective antagonist, GSK‐343, downregulated gradually EZH2 at the doses of 5 and 10 mg/kg, compared to the SCI group. While the lower dose of 1 mg/kg did not significantly reduce EZH2 levels compared to SCI‐induced animals. Since EZH2 is responsible for the methylation of H3K27, we analyzed the effect of the inhibitor GSK‐343 on the modulation of this epigenetic modification following SCI. Our data show a marked increase in H3K27Me2 levels in mice subjected to SCI compared to the sham group. Treatment with GSK‐343, at all doses, significantly reduced H3K27Me2 levels compared to the untreated SCI group (Figure 3B, densitometric analysis B1). To further investigate the EZH2 pathway, we performed western blot analysis of related proteins such as TNF receptor‐associated factor 6 (TRAF6), nuclear factor of kappa light polypeptide gene enhancer in b‐cells inhibitor alpha (IκBα), and NF‐κB. Our results demonstrated that TRAF 6 levels were significantly increased following SCI, compared to control animals, while GSK‐343 administration at the highest doses of 5 and 10 mg/kg, notably reduced TRAF6 expression compared to SCI‐induced mice (Figure 3C, densitometric analysis C1). Moreover, our data showed that IκBα protein levels were reduced in SCI mice compared with sham and were dose‐dependently increased by GSK‐343 (Figure 3D, densitometric analysis D1). Conversely, in the SCI‐group mice, there was a significant increase in nuclear NF‐κB levels compared to sham mice. GSK‐343 treatment at the doses of 5 mg/kg and 10 mg/kg significantly attenuated NF‐κB levels compared to animals injured by the SCI procedure (Figure 3E, densitometric analysis E1). Overall, these findings give us the possibility to consider treatment with GSK‐343 as a powerful modulator of the pro‐inflammatory pathway when administered at doses of 5 and 10 mg/kg.

sec.title: GSK‐343 Treatments Reduced Pro‐Inflammatory Markers
sec.p: Activation of NF‐κB promotes transcription of pro‐inflammatory genes resulting in increased levels of pro‐inflammatory enzymes and pro‐inflammatory cytokines which contribute to the neuroinflammation during SCI (Liu et al. 2017). For this purpose, Western blot analysis was conducted on the cytosolic fraction by detecting inflammatory enzymes like cyclooxygenase‐2 (COX‐2) and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS), TNF‐α, IL‐1β, and IL‐17. Our results demonstrated high levels of both iNOS and COX‐2 in samples of mice subjected to SCI procedure compared with the physiological levels of the sham mice (Figure 4A,B, densitometric analysis A1, B1). Intraperitoneal administration of GSK‐343 at a dose of 1 mg/kg did not produce appreciable beneficial effects to reduce these levels, however, higher doses of 5 mg/kg and even more the dose of 10 mg/kg, showed a significant reduction of both enzymes iNOS and COX‐2 compared to SCI mice (Figure 4A,B, densitometric analysis A1, B1). Moreover, in all the analyses the SCI mice showed high levels of proinflammatory cytokines TNF‐α, IL‐1β and IL‐17 compared to sham mice. The treatment with GSK‐343 (5 and 10 mg/kg) was able to reduce the expression of TNF‐α (Figure 4C, densitometric analysis C1), IL‐1β (Figure 4D, densitometric analysis D1) and IL‐17 (Figure 4E, densitometric analysis E1). Otherwise, the 1 mg/kg dose was ineffective in restoring these neuroinflammatory markers.

sec.p: The primary cells contributing to the inflammatory response are microglia and astrocytes, which have also been linked to the production of pain following injury (Kisucka et al. 2021). Immunofluorescence analysis of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ionized calcium‐binding adaptor molecule‐1 (IBA‐1) demonstrated that the SCI procedure leads to a significant increase in the number of cells positive for both markers (Figure 6B,H; score F and L) compared to sham mice (Figure 5A–G; F and L score). sec.title: GSK‐343 Administration Reduced Mast Cell Infiltration Following SCI
sec.p: Mast cells are effector cells in the immune and inflammatory system, implicated in neuroinflammation (Dong et al. 2014). To investigate the protective effect of GSK‐343 on mast cell infiltration and activation, spinal cord tissues were stained by toluidine blu dye. Our results demonstrated an elevated number of mast cells in SCI tissue (Figure 6B, F score), compared to sham mice (Figure 6A, F score). The dose of GSK‐343 1 mg/kg was unable to significantly reduce the number of mast cells after SCI (Figure 6C, score F). In contrast, the number of mast cells was significantly reduced in spinal cord sections from mice treated with GSK‐343 at doses of 5 mg/kg (Figure 6D, score F) and 10 mg/kg (Figure 6E,F) compared to SCI mice.

sec.title: GSK‐343 Treatments Reduced Markers of the Innate Immune System
sec.p: The latest analysis aimed to deepen the link between the inhibition of EZH2 and the innate immune system. Therefore, we performed western blot analysis for the evaluation of CD45, ELISA assay for the study of MCP‐1 and finally immunohistochemistry to analyze the tissue expression of CD68 in the perilesional area. CD45 is involved in innate immune cell regulation and communication between immune cells. Moreover, immediately after SCI, a large number of CD45 inflammatory cells infiltrated the lesion area and led to the secondary damage of neural tissue (Fisher et al. 2022). Results from western blot analyses demonstrated that CD45 levels were significantly increased in SCI mice (Figure 7A, densitometric analysis A1) compared to the sham mice (Figure 7A, densitometric analysis A1). GSK‐343 administration (1, 5, and 10 mg/kg) significantly reduced the levels of CD45 in a dose‐dependent manner compared to SCI mice (Figure 7A, densitometric analysis A1). Also, the marker MCP‐1 is associated with the activation of the innate immune system (Kim et al. 2022). Our results demonstrated that GSK‐343 (1, 5, and 10 mg/kg) significantly reduced the levels of MCP‐1 (Figure 7B), compared to the SCI group. In response to inflammatory stimuli, MCP‐1 is secreted by various cell types, including macrophages (Kobayakawa et al. 2019). Therefore, to confirm the protective effect of GSK‐343 in the modulation of these innate immune cells, we investigated the number of positive cells for CD68, a marker expressed in macrophages. The immunohistochemistry of the perilesional area revealed an elevated number of CD68+ cells in the SCI group (Figure 7D, D1, score H), compared to the control group (Figure 7C, C1, score H). The 1 mg/kg dose of GSK‐343 significantly reduced the immunopositive count (Figure 8E, E1, H score). More significant results were obtained following treatments with GSK‐343 at doses of 5 mg/kg (Figure 8F, F1, H score) and 10 mg/kg (Figure 8G, G1, H score), that significantly reduced the number of CD68 positive cells, restoring a condition similar to sham animals.

sec.title: GSK‐343 Treatment Improved Locomotor Recovery After SCI
sec.p: To evaluate whether SCI was associated with motor deficits and to determine the potential functional benefits of GSK‐343, open‐field locomotor performance was assessed using the BMS for 10 days post‐injury (Figure 8). Sham mice maintained normal motor function throughout the observation period, whereas SCI animals exhibited marked hindlimb paralysis and significantly reduced BMS scores. Treatment with GSK‐343 at 1 mg/kg did not produce measurable improvement compared with the SCI group. Conversely, administration of GSK‐343 at 5 and 10 mg/kg resulted in a progressive and significant recovery of locomotor function, with higher BMS scores evident from days 4 and 3, respectively, relative to untreated SCI mice (Figure 8).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: After spinal cord injury, there is a sudden upregulation of inflammatory mediators which determine potential harmful consequences such as disruption of the BBB, demyelination, and axonal damage (Rice et al. 2007). Furthermore, the innate immune system also plays a key role during SCI, in fact, within 24 h of SCI, there is a rapid migration of innate immune cells from the peripheral blood which can participate in the damage of the local microenvironment and contribute to long‐term complications (Zrzavy et al. 2021). Following acute injury, prolonged immune dysregulation could exacerbate neuroinflammation and neurological dysfunction thus worsening tissue damage (Schwab et al. 2014).

Recent studies on epigenetic mechanisms have demonstrated that DNA methylation and post‐translational modifications of histones, key regulator of gene expression or repression in most tissues, are closely involved in neuroinflammation processes. Among this, EZH2, an essential component of PRC2, has drawn significant attention for its role in neurological diseases (Luo et al. 2020; Wang, Qin, et al. 2020). In pre‐clinical models of neuropathic pain, EZH2 levels are significantly increased in combination with neuroinflammation processes. In addition, it was demonstrated that acute SCI increase EZH2 and H3K27me3 protein expression in the spinal cord, thus suggesting its possible role in the pathogenesis of SCI (Ni et al. 2021). Therefore, using a murine model of acute SCI, we investigated for the first time how EZH2 inhibition, mediated by GSK‐343, could modulate key acute pathogenetic mechanisms of spinal cord trauma.

Behavioral motor impairment associated with SCI can include a variety of symptoms and dysfunctions, such as loss of sensation, partial or complete paralysis of the limbs, and changes in muscle tone that significantly impact mobility (Perrouin‐Verbe et al. 2021). Spinal cord compression also leads to subsequent neuronal degeneration, demyelination, and accumulation of neutrophils in situ (Hassannejad et al. 2019). Our finding demonstrated that treatment with GSK‐343 exerted a significant protective effect, as evidenced by the improvement of the tissue architecture of the spinal cord and the restoration of myelinated neurons. Although the role of EZH2 in neuroinflammation is well documented, there are few studies on EZH2‐mediated inflammation after SCI. Shuangfei Ni et al. (Ni et al. 2021) reported EZH2 overexpression in rats with acute SCI, and in line with their findings, our data confirm that EZH2 is upregulated after SCI, suggesting its active participation in the secondary injury cascade.

Several studies investigating the EZH2 pathway have demonstrated that this methyltransferase acts upstream of the NF‐κB‐mediated inflammatory signaling pathway (Luo et al. 2020; Kaur et al. 2023). Specifically, EZH2 promotes the activation of TRAF6 which, by degrading the inhibitory protein IκBα, activates NF‐κB, thus contributing to the neuroinflammatory process. Since that, we confirmed the involvement of the TRAF6/NF‐κB/IκBα pathway, demonstrating that EZH2 inhibition, by GSK‐343, attenuates neuroinflammation through modulation of this signaling pathway. After SCI, activated NF‐kB rapidly translocates into the nucleus and increases the expression of pro‐inflammatory genes, including those encoding pro‐inflammatory cytokines and enzymes that contribute to the worsening of pathological conditions. In this regard, our data highlighted that the upstream inhibition of EZH2 and its signaling pathway, mediated by intraperitoneal administration of GSK‐343, was capable of reducing pro‐inflammatory markers such as cytokines TNF‐a, IL‐1b, and IL‐17 and enzymes such as iNOS and COX‐2, thereby reducing neuroinflammation after SCI. Pro‐inflammatory cytokines released after NF‐κB activation are major components of the innate immunity and inflammatory response after SCI. Within 24 h of injury, these cytokines can activate resident immune cells such as microglial cells and attract circulating immune cells such as mast cells to the site of injury. In this context, increased expression of EZH2 in the CNS was recently found to be an important contributor to microglial activation in rats with neuropathic pain (Yadav and Weng 2017). Furthermore, it was demonstrated that EZH2 was co‐localized in LPS‐stimulated microglia and astrocytes, so it may play an essential role in cell‐mediated innate immunity (Zhang et al. 2021). Based on this evidence, we reported that after GSK‐343 treatments, the expression of GFAP and Iba‐1 led to a decrease in reactive astrocytes and microglia after SCI.

During tissue damage, the physiological homeostasis between mast cells and glial cells is interrupted with a consequent delay in functional recovery (Skaper et al. 2014). Accordingly, we observed a substantial increase in mast cell number following SCI, however, administration of GSK‐343 was highly effective in reducing mast cell infiltration. These findings align with previous studies highlighting the key role of EZH2 in the pathogenesis of spinal cord injury. In particular, a recent study demonstrated that BMSC‐derived exosomes carrying miR‐26a‐5p ameliorate SCI by negatively regulating EZH2 and activating the BDNF–TrkB‐CREB signaling pathway. While that approach modulates EZH2 expression at the post‐transcriptional level, our results support a complementary pharmacological strategy, in which the selective EZH2 inhibitor GSK‐343 directly suppresses the TRAF6/IκBα/NF‐κB signaling cascade. Both mechanisms ultimately converge on reducing neuroinflammation and glial activation, reinforcing the pivotal role of EZH2 as a therapeutic target for limiting secondary injury after SCI (Chen et al. 2024).

In the context of innate immunity during SCI, the investigation of the surface protein CD45 is often used to study infiltrating leukocytes and the glycoprotein CD68 to study activated macrophages. In fact, after SCI, the destruction of the BBB and the consequent infiltration of inflammatory cells leads to the formation of numerous subsets of immune cells that promote damage to the spinal cord (Li et al. 2022). Regarding EZH2, growing evidence points to the activity of this epigenetic enzyme as an important mechanism for regulating macrophage/microglia activation and polarization (Zhang et al. 2018; Wang et al. 2022). This observation suggested that EZH2 is an epigenetic regulator involved in the immunomodulatory regulation of macrophages. Therefore, we hypothesized that EZH2 inhibition may modulate macrophage migration during SCI. According to the results obtained, we observed that GSK‐343 was able to reduce the number of CD68‐positive cells and CD45 levels in spinal cord tissues subjected to SCI. Furthermore, the administration of GSK‐343 in mice with SCI also reduced the levels of MCP‐1, a cytokine involved in chemotaxis and attraction of monocytes and macrophages to inflammation sites.

Overall, these data demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of EZH2, with GSK‐343 inhibitor, modulated the TRAF6/NF‐κB/IκBα pathway, reduced numerous pro‐inflammatory markers, and modulated the innate immune response. However, it remains to be explored whether the mechanism by which GSK343 attenuates the neuroinflammatory and immune response is related to the TRAF6/NF‐κB pathway or whether it is related to a direct mechanism with innate immunity cells of the CNS.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, we demonstrated for the first time that GSK‐343, an EZH2 inhibitor, could be considered a promising therapeutic strategy for the management of SCI, thanks to its ability to modulate the TRAF6/NFKB pathway, counteract neuroinflammation and hyperactivation of innate immune cells. However, despite the promising results obtained in this study, several limitations need to be addressed. First, preclinical models are not always able to fully mimic human diseases in a translational manner. Differences in neuroinflammation processes and activation of innate immunity between mice and humans should be considered. Furthermore, the use of more complex techniques will be able to better validate these preliminary results, thus providing a more robust characterization of the efficacy of GSK‐343 in SCI. Considering this, future studies using in vitro gene silencing models or in vivo knockout models will be able to establish in detail the role of EZH2 in the context of SCI.
